Cancer survival rates in the United States vary widely depending on the type of cancer, the stage at diagnosis, and how well it responds to treatment. Five-year survival is a common benchmark, but it is only an average and does not predict any one person’s outcome. In general, cancers that are usually found early or treated effectively have much higher survival rates, while cancers that tend to spread before diagnosis have much lower ones.

- Bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) — about 8,000 cases/year in the United States
- Bone and joint cancer — about 3,900 cases/year
- Anal cancer — about 9,700 cases/year
- Testicular cancer — about 9,900 cases/year
- Hodgkin lymphoma — about 10,500 cases/year
